d: Add details, as to an account or idea; clarify the meaning of and discourse in a learned way, usually in writing
r: Latin expatior, from ex- + spatior “walk about”
s: “It can't fly,” he expatiated. “It can move forward only by hopping.”
old_f: Leave one’s homeland, as to work abroad; settle permanently in a foreign country, usually for reasons of employment
Make amends for, as for a sin or crime; atone through suffering or penance, usually in a religious setting
Breathe out, as from the lungs; release air slowly and steadily, usually while singing
ety: From the participle stem of Latin expatior, from ex- + spatior (“walk about”).

d: Written in the form of or carried on by letters or correspondence
r: Latin epistolārius, from epistola “letter”
s: Bram Stoker's novel Dracula (1897) is written in epistolary style.
old_f: Delivered in the form of or set down as a formal public sermon
Arranged in the form of or composed as a set of short poems
Relating to the duties of or carried out by a bishop or archbishop
ety: 1627, from Latin epistolārius, from epistola (“letter”) (English epistle) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ) from ἐπιστέλλω (epistéllō, “to send a message”) from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to prepare, send”). For the noun, compare Middle English pistelarie and Old English pistelari, both from Medieval Latin epistolārium, possibly via an unattested *epistelari, *epistolarie.

d: Containing or implying a slight or showing prejudice
r: Latin invidiōsus, from invidia “envy, ill will”; a doublet of envious
s: But the rich man—not to make any invidious comparison—is always sold to the institution which makes him rich.
old_f: Containing or giving a feeling of new energy
Hidden or impossible to see with the eye
Relating to the private life of an individual
ety: Borrowed from Latin invidiōsus, from invidia (“envy, ill will”), from in- (“upon”) + videō (“to see”); the meaning developed from “look back at” to “look askance at” to “envy.” Doublet of envious, from Old French.

d: A flowery and highly rhetorical oration
r: Latin perōrō “to speak at length, conclude a speech”, from per- “very” + ōrō “to speak”
s: Nephew, what means this passionate discourse, This peroration with such circumstance?
old_f: A small hole bored through a plank
A long walk around a boundary
A bitter draught given before surgery
ety: From Latin perōrō (“to speak at length, to conclude a speech”) (from per- (“very”) + ōrō (“to speak, to orate”) (English orate)) + -ation (“action (nominalizer)”) (from Latin -ātiō).

d: Related by blood
r: Latin cōnsanguineus, from con- “together” + sanguis “blood”
s: Am not I consanguineous? am I not of her blood?
old_f: Bright red in color
Sharing one opinion
Living under one roof
ety: Adapted borrowing of Latin cōnsanguineus + -ous, from con- (“together”) + sanguineus (“of or pertaining to blood”), from sanguis (“blood”). By surface analysis, con- + sanguineous. Doublet of consanguine.

d: A visible (but not necessarily material) manifestation of a deity to a human person
r: Late Latin theophania, from Greek theós “God” + phaínō “to shine, appear”
s: It was a bewildering theophany, since it was impossible to make out anything clearly in the stormy obscurity of thunder, lightning, smoke and wind.
old_f: A spoken (but not necessarily public) declaration of faith made before a congregation
A written (but not necessarily signed) record of a meeting held by church elders
A sudden (but not necessarily lasting) loss of religious belief in a devout person
ety: From Late Latin theophania, corresponding to theo- + -phany, from θεός (theós, “God”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).

d: A large galleon sailed in the Mediterranean as a merchantman
r: French caraque, from Latin carrus “wagon”; or perhaps from Arabic qarāqīr
s: Thereafter huge sailing carracks brought Indian pepper and cotton, Indonesian perfume and spice, Chinese silk and porcelain, to the royal trading house at Lisbon.
old_f: A small lean-to built against a castle wall as a stable
A heavy wagon pulled through the Alps to haul supplies
A narrow canal dug through the marshes as a trade route
ety: From French caraque (compare Spanish and Portuguese carraca, Italian caracca), from Latin carraca, from Latin carrus (“wagon”); or perhaps from Arabic قَرَاقِير (qarāqīr).

d: A woman’s silk or lace scarf
r: Spanish mantilla “large veil; small cape”, from manta “blanket, cloth”
s: The Duchess of Alba wrapped herself in a mantilla coat.
old_f: A man’s fur or leather cap
A child’s wool or cotton mitten
A priest’s gold or silver chalice
ety: Borrowed from Spanish mantilla (“large veil; small cape”), from manta (“blanket, cloth, cloth banner”) + -illa (diminutive).

d: Indicator provided by the stationary arm whose shadow indicates the time on the sundial
r: Greek gnṓmōn “discerner, interpreter; carpenter’s square”
s: The little style or gnomon, which being fixed on the pole of the globe, and turning round with it, points out the hours upon the hour circle.
old_f: Small figure made of carved stone that stands guard in a garden to bring good luck
Brief saying or maxim that is engraved on a coin or medal to honor a ruler
Curved blade attached to the end of a pole that is used to prune high branches
ety: Borrowed from French gnomon, or directly from its etymon Latin gnōmōn, or directly from its etymon Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn, “discerner, interpreter; carpenter’s square; gnomon of a sundial; (geometry) gnomon”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to be aware of; to perceive; to know”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”); the word is thus related to know. The geometry sense (sense 4) is from the resemblance of the plane figure to a carpenter’s square. Similarly, a gnomon in mathematics (sense 5) is also shaped like a carpenter’s square when depicted pictorially if the figurate n

d: Full of trivial conversation
r: Latin garrulus “talkative”, from garriō “to chatter”
s: She lingered for a few moments, and was garrulous over some detail of the household.
old_f: Full of garlic
Gripping by the throat
Fond of fine clothing
ety: Adapted borrowing of Latin garrulus (“talkative”) + -ous, from the verb garriō (“to chatter”).

d: Stubbornly persistent in wrongdoing
r: Latin obdūrātus “hardened”, from ob- “against” + dūrō “to harden”
s: But custom maketh blind and obdurate The loftiest hearts.
old_f: Lasting for a long time
Gloomy and overcast
Hard to see through
ety: First attested in the 1450s, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English obdurat(e), borrowed from Latin obdūrātus (“hardened”), perfect passive participle of obdūrō (“to harden”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ob- (“against”) + dūrō (“to harden, render hard”), from dūrus (“hard”). Compare durable, endure.

d: Having the power to prevent evil or bad luck
r: Greek apotrópaios, from apó “away” + trópos “turn”: “turning away evil”
s: A boring subtext, about the wisdom or otherwise of actually uttering Voldemort's name, meanwhile robs the apotropaic device of its force.
old_f: Having the habit of turning toward the sun
Having the shape of a coiled spiral shell
Having the power to cure fever and chills
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀποτρόπαιος (apotrópaios), from ἀπό (apó, “away”) and τρόπος (trópos, “turn”); thus meaning “causing things to turn away”, as in “turns away evil”.

d: (of liquids) clouded as with sediment
r: Latin turbidus “disturbed”, from turba “tumult, disturbance”
s: This makes the estimation of the refractive index of the turbid liquid quite problematic.
old_f: (of winds) blowing in sudden gusts
(of fabric) wound around the head
(of soil) heavy with peat
ety: From Middle English turbide, borrowed from Latin turbidus (“disturbed”), from turba (“mass, throng, crowd, tumult, disturbance”).

d: A carving or line drawing on rock (especially one made by prehistoric people)
r: French pétroglyphe, from Greek pétra “rock” + gluphḗ “carved work”
s: The petroglyphs of Central Asia form a long sequence from the Neolithic onwards.
old_f: A layer of fossil fuel trapped in rock (especially beneath an ancient seabed)
A sweet resin that hardens into amber (especially along northern coasts)
A large boulder carried by glaciers (especially one left standing alone on a plain)
ety: From French pétroglyphe, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “rock”) + γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carved work”). By surface analysis, petro- + glyph.

d: A person addicted to luxury and pleasures of the senses
r: Late Latin voluptuārius, from Latin voluptās “delight, pleasure”
s: Another Greek, the historian Megacleides, singles out Heracles as the supreme voluptuary.
old_f: A person who serves in the army without being paid
A person who writes many long books on one subject
A person who studies the eruptions of volcanoes
ety: From French voluptuaire, or directly from its etymon Late Latin voluptuārius, from Latin voluptārius (“pleasure-seeker; agreeable, delightful, pleasant; sensual”), from voluptās (“delight, pleasure, satisfaction”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns). Voluptās is derived from volup (“with pleasure; agreeably, pleasantly, satisfactorily”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose; to want”)) + -tās (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns indicating a state of being).

d: Unrestrained, especially with regard to feelings
r: Middle English overweninge: overween + -ing
s: She wins one modeling contest in Montana and suddenly she’s overweening.
old_f: Overgrown, especially with regard to weeds
Underfed, especially with regard to newborn animals
Overcast, especially with regard to winter skies
ety: From Middle English overweninge, equivalent to overween + -ing. Cognate with obsolete Dutch overwanig, overwaand (“presumptuous; cocky; conceited”).

d: A dusty wind from the Sahara that blows toward the western coast of Africa during the winter
r: Twi (Akan) haramata
s: Okonkwo's fame had grown like a bush-fire in the harmattan.
old_f: A woven grass mat from the Sahel that is used to shade the doorways of mud houses during the dry season
A stringed instrument from the Sahara that is played by wandering poets at weddings and festivals
A tall headdress from the Sahara that is worn by camel drivers to protect the face from sand
ety: From Twi Akan haramata or a related word (whence also Spanish harmatán). The ultimate origin is supposed by some to be an Arabic word, but which one is uncertain; حَرَام (ḥarām, “accursed thing”) has been suggested.

d: A gaping grimace
r: Latin rictus
s: His face was a rictus of sheer delight.
old_f: A sudden chill
A Roman tax
A narrow crack
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin rictus.

d: Purported; commonly put forth or accepted as true on inconclusive grounds
r: Latin putātīvus “supposed, purported”, from putō “to think, consider”
s: In answer to the objection, that if a thing is only putative, it is fictitious.
old_f: Penal; commonly imposed or carried out as a punishment for minor offenses
Rotten; commonly found or left to decay in damp and airless places
Graceful; commonly praised or admired for its smooth and polished finish
ety: First attested c. 1432, from Middle French putatif, from Latin putātīvus (“supposed, purported”), from putātus (“thought”), from putō (“to think, to consider, to reckon”).

d: Someone who takes spoils or plunder (as in war)
r: Dutch vrijbuiter “free booty-er”; a doublet of filibuster
s: The time-honoured connection between forest and freebooter.
old_f: Someone who travels without paying fares (as on trains)
Someone who repairs boots and shoes (as in villages)
Someone who frees prisoners for ransom (as in feudal times)
ety: From free + booty + -er. Calque of Dutch vrijbuiter (literally “free booty-er”), from vrij (“free”) + buit (“booty”) + -er (occupational suffix). Doublet of filibuster.

d: The sound of an alarm (usually a bell)
r: Old Occitan tocasenh, from tocar “strike, touch” + senh “bell”
s: I'll ring the tocsin, I'll have Saint-Antoine out.
old_f: A poison made from snake venom
A small brass drum (usually Turkish)
A toast to the bride
ety: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French toquesain (modern tocsin), from Old Occitan tocasenh, from tocar (“strike, touch”) + senh (“bell”).

d: Taking on different forms
r: Proteus + -an, after the Greek sea god who could change his shape
s: An amoeba is a protean animalcule.
old_f: Rich in meat and eggs
Lasting through many ages
Leaning slightly forward
ety: From Proteus + -an, referring to the Greek warden of sea-beasts, renowned for his ability to change shape.

d: (of the voice) quivering as from weakness or fear
r: Latin tremulus, from tremō “to tremble, shake”
s: The trying nature of his position drove the blood from his cheek, and made his lips tremulous.
old_f: (of the voice) loud and booming as from a great hall
(of the voice) flat and dull as from long repetition
(of the voice) smooth and rich as from careful training
ety: From Latin tremulus, from tremō (“to tremble, shake”) + -ulus. Doublet of tremor and tremble. By surface analysis, tremulate + -ous.

d: A familiar name for a person (often a shortened version of a person’s given name)
r: Latin cognōmen, from con- “with” + nōmen “name”
s: Gaius was his praenomen or forename, Iulius his nomen or surname, and Caesar his cognomen.
old_f: A secret sign used by members of a society (often a gesture or a handshake)
A small cog or gear in a clockwork mechanism (often made of brass)
A personal motto inscribed on a coat of arms (often written in Latin)
ety: From Latin cognōmen, from con- (“with”) + nōmen (“name; family name”).

d: So great in size or force or extent as to elicit awe
r: Latin prōdigiōsus “strange, marvellous”, from prōdigium “omen, portent, wonder”
s: A prodigious quantity of insects of all sorts (but no mosquitoes) assailed us at our evening meal.
old_f: So wasteful of money or goods as to bring ruin upon oneself
So clever at an early age as to astonish one’s elders
So precise in manners and speech as to seem stiff
ety: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English prodigious (“warning of disaster, portentous”), from Latin prōdigiōsus (“strange, unnatural; marvellous, wonderful, prodigious”), from prōdigium (“prophetic sign, omen, portent; prodigy, wonder”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of’ forming adjectives from nouns). Prōdigium is derived from prō- (prefix denoting a forward direction, something before or prior, or prominence) + aiō (“to say, speak”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵ- (“to say”)) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns). The English word is analysable as prodigy + -ous. The adv

d: Eager to acquire and possess things especially material possessions or ideas
r: Latin acquīsītus “acquired, gained”
s: She has an acquisitive nature.
old_f: Eager to question and examine things especially unfamiliar customs or beliefs
Tending to agree and comply readily especially with requests from those in authority
Able to hear and distinguish sounds especially very faint or distant noises
ety: From an alteration of Latin acquisītus (“acquired, gained”), or possibly from acquisite + -ive.

d: A small gift (especially one given by a merchant to a customer who makes a purchase)
r: Louisiana French, from Spanish la ñapa, from Quechua yapa “addition, increase”
s: Call it a little lagniappe, goodbuddy.
old_f: A small boat (especially one used by fishermen to set crab traps in shallow bayous)
A spicy stew (especially one made with shellfish and served over rice at festivals)
A rowdy dance (especially one held in a barn to celebrate the end of the harvest)
ety: Borrowed from Louisiana French lagniappe, from Spanish la ñapa, a variant of yapa (“small gift or additional quantity given to a valued customer”), from Quechua yapa (“addition, increase, supplement; lagniappe”), yapay (“to add, to increase”).

d: A manner of speaking that is natural to native speakers of a language
r: Anglo-Norman parlance, from parler “to talk” + -ance
s: We approach the contest, still known in the common parlance of the country, as "the first Pennimite War."
old_f: A long pole with a sharp blade carried by foot soldiers in medieval armies
A formal assembly of nobles and clergy summoned by a king to approve taxes
A small sitting room set aside for receiving guests in a large house
ety: From Middle English *parlaunce, from Anglo-Norman parlance, parlaunce, from parler (“to talk”) + -ance.

d: A person holding a fief; a person who owes allegiance and service to a feudal lord
r: Medieval Latin vassallus “manservant, retainer”, from Gaulish *wassos “young man, squire”
s: The king ordered his vassals to join him on the crusade unless they had a written note signed by the archbishop or pope.
old_f: A vessel used for washing; a basin of metal or stone set before guests at a feast
A servant who carves meat; an attendant who waits at the high table during a banquet
A soldier who guards a castle; a man who keeps watch on the walls during the night
ety: From Middle English vassal, from Old French vassal, from Medieval Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from Latin vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and Welsh gwas).

d: Inactivity resulting from a dislike of work
r: Latin indolentia “freedom from pain; insensibility”
s: Her whole figure expressed a tense vibrant life in singular contrast to the apparent indolence of the men at whom she was talking.
old_f: Sadness resulting from the loss of a loved one
Rudeness resulting from a lack of proper upbringing
Wealth resulting from a large inheritance
ety: Borrowed from Middle French indolence, or from its etymon Latin indolentia (“freedom from pain; insensibility”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + dolēns (“hurting, suffering; grieving, lamenting”) + -ia (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns). Dolēns is the present participle of doleō (“to hurt, suffer; to be sorry, deplore, grieve for, lament”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to divide, split”).

d: Marked by lack of definite plan or regularity or purpose; jumping from one thing to another
r: Latin dēsultōrius “hasty, superficial”, from dēsultor “a circus rider who jumped from horse to horse”
s: I teach a class of desultory minds.
old_f: Marked by an excess of formal politeness or ceremony; bowing and scraping at every turn
Marked by dry, barren, or lifeless landscapes; stretching on without water or shade
Marked by a deep sense of guilt or regret; brooding over one past mistake
ety: From Latin dēsultōrius (“hasty, casual, superficial”), from dēsultor (“a circus rider who jumped from one galloping horse to another”), from dēsiliō (“jump down”), from dē (“down”) + saliō (“jump, leap”).

d: Poor enough to need help from others
r: Necessity + -ous, after Middle French nécessiteux
s: But it is to be given to our necessitous kindred, or in charity.
old_f: Required by law in every case
Fond of strict routines and habits
Cruel enough to cause harm to others
ety: From necessity + -ous, after Middle French nécessiteux.

d: A glass container used to store and display items in a shop or museum or home
r: French vitrine, from vitre “pane of glass”, from Latin vitrum “glass”
s: The dealer was trying to concentrate on showing Bouck some small art-glass pieces in a vitrine in the middle of the booth.
old_f: A sour liquid made from wine or cider used to pickle vegetables or dress salads at home
A climbing plant grown against a wall or trellis to shade a terrace or courtyard
A narrow strip of stained glass set into a church window to depict a saint
ety: Borrowed from French vitrine, from vitre (“pane of glass”), from Old French, from Latin vitrum (“glass”).

d: Greatly exceeding bounds of reason or moderation
r: Usury + -ous
s: The originator of a usurious loan in California is subject to severe civil penalties.
old_f: Relating to the right to use another’s property
Tending to take power by force
Commonly done or accepted as normal
ety: From usury + -ous.

d: Causing irritation or annoyance
r: Nettle + -some
s: My old car is very nettlesome.
old_f: Neat and orderly
Small and sharp
Fond of nesting
ety: From nettle + -some.

d: A feeling of alarm or dread
r: Latin trepidātiō, from trepidō “be agitated”
s: I decided, with considerable trepidation, to let him drive my car without me.
old_f: A long walk through rough country
A three-legged frame for a camera
A slow rise in the price of grain
ety: Borrowed from Latin trepidātiō, from trepidō (“be agitated”).

d: Marked by excessive self-indulgence and moral decay
r: Latin effētus “exhausted”, literally “that has given birth”
s: Most writers merely produce effete works on paper, you might say, but Kerouac went and wrestled with the tree itself.
old_f: Marked by sudden bursts of great energy
Marked by a strong and lasting impact
Marked by careless and untidy dress
ety: From Latin effētus (“exhausted”, literally “that has given birth”), 1620s.

d: Break apart or in two, using violence
r: Old English sundrian “to separate, split, part, divide”
s: In Taran's hand the sundered bone had turned into gray dust, which he cast aside.
old_f: Dry out under strong sun, using racks
Sink below water, using weights
Bury deep under ground, using a spade
ety: From Middle English sundren (“to separate, part, divide”), from Old English sundrian (“to separate, split, part, divide”), from Proto-Germanic *sundrōną (“to separate”), from Proto-Indo-European *sen(e)- (“separate, without”). Cognate with Scots sinder, sunder (“to separate, divide, split up”), Dutch zonderen (“to isolate”), German sondern (“to separate”), Swedish söndra (“to divide”). More at sundry.

d: Habitually reserved and uncommunicative
r: Latin taciturnus, from tacitus “secret, tacit”
s: The two sisters could hardly have been more different, one so boisterous and expressive, the other so taciturn and calm.
old_f: Sticky to the touch
Quick to change direction
Easily turned aside
ety: Back-formation from taciturnity, from Middle English taciturnite, from Latin taciturnitās; or alternatively from French taciturne, likely reinforced by Latin taciturnus, from tacitus (“secret, tacit”).

d: Express strong disapproval of
r: Late Latin excoriō “to take the skin or hide off”
s: The teacher continued to excoriate the student after his academic issues.
old_f: Remove the core from
Drive out evil spirits
Dig out by scooping
ety: First attested in the first part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English *excoriaten (only attested in its past participle), borrowed from Late Latin excoriātus perfect passive participle of excoriō (“to take the skin or hide off, flay, skin”), from ex- (“out off, from”) + corium (“hide, skin”) + -ō. Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English, later archaic.
